newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba admits Helms-Burton hurts, but says not fatal.
newsitem.headline: Cuba admits Helms-Burton hurts, but says not fatal.

text.p: One year after President Bill Clinton approved the controversial Helms-Burton law to toughen Washington's longstanding embargo against Cuba, Fidel Castro's government says the legislation may have hurt but it has not inflicted fatal damage to the economy.
"This law is condemned to failure, it's useless," said parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon in an interview published by the ruling Communist Party daily Granma on Tuesday.

"They (the United States) will never succeed in getting the Cuban people or the rest of the world to bend to their arrogance," added Alarcon, a former foreign minister who is Cuba's most vocal spokesman on U.S. affairs.

Clinton set aside previous reservations and signed the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act into law after Cuban MiG fighters shot down two small private U.S. planes off Cuba, killing the four Cuban-American crew, on Feb. 24, 1996.

Widely known as Helms-Burton after its Republican sponsors Jesse Helms and Dan Burton, the law codifies Washington's 35- year embargo on Cuba and demands radical political change and the dumping of President Castro as a condition for normal bilateral relations. And it includes provisions to punish some foreign firms doing business on the island.

Those clauses, contained in Titles III and IV, aimed to curb the foreign investment Cuba needs to revive its fragile economy. They provoked intense irritation among U.S. allies such as Canada and the European Union. And among foreign companies investing in Cuba, they appeared to inspire anxiety rather than panic.
"It (Helms-Burton) has inflicted damage but it will not kill us," Francisco Soberon, the president of Cuba's central bank, told reporters last week.
Authorities say the law slowed credits to Cuba and caused future investors to hesitate, but did not prompt an exodus.
"Most people wanted to assess its effects," Soberon said. "That created delays and affected the cash-flow. But we always have a tense balance in short-term liquidity," Soberon added.

"It's very hard to quantify the damage," said Cuba's Deputy President Carlos Lage. But he acknowledged that the 1996-97 sugar cane harvest began late because of delays to foreign financing for technical input.
Two high-profile investors have been punished so far under Helms-Burton -- Mexican telecommunications firm Grupo Domos and Canadian mining concern Sherritt International.

They were sanctioned under Title IV, by which senior executives of foreign firms deemed to be "trafficking" in property expropriated after Castro's 1959 revolution may be barred entry to the United States.

Both Sherritt and Domos said they would stay on in Cuba. But Domos recently has been reported to be reducing its presence for unrelated reasons, selling off part of its stake in a telecommunications investment to Italian firm STET.

Washington also has sent several warning letters. One firm, a Panamanian company selling Mitsubishi and other vehicles in Havana, received a warning in January, apparently over its office premises. Motores Internacionales del Caribe S.A. (MICSA), said last month the problem was probably resolved because it had moved its office. But MICSA added that it moved not because of the threat but because it needed more office space.

Title III, under which U.S. citizens or firms may bring lawsuits against foreign firms "trafficking" in nationalized property, remains under wraps. Clinton has twice suspended for six months its implementation. U.S. allies welcomed the waivers but still want Title III scrapped.

Helms-Burton has caused some foreign firms to restructure their business in Cuba. The ING bank of the Netherlands, for example, withdrew last year from direct financing for the sugar industry, but remained in other sectors.

Cuban authorities say it is hard to judge how many prospective firms may have been deterred by Helms-Burton. Foreign Investment Minister Ibrahim Ferradaz said that since the law came into effect, some 42 new joint ventures have been set up, meaning there are now more than 260 such ventures.

The law appears to have hardened Havana's resolve not to change course. "Helms-Burton ... mobilized Cubans to defend sovereignty, independence and their society and to close the door to any attempt to impose a return to the past," Alarcon said.
